title: pgvector & AI Vector Embeddings
description: Store high-dimensional vector embeddings, perform cosine/L2 distance similarity searches, and build RAG pipelines with HNSW and IVFFlat.

data.text: **`pgvector`** is an open-source PostgreSQL extension that adds native support for high-dimensional vector embeddings generated by AI models (OpenAI, HuggingFace, Cohere). It turns PostgreSQL into a high-performance vector database for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and semantic search.

rows: Industry standard for production AI apps

data.title: Semantic Vector Search with HNSW Cosine Distance
data.content: Finding the top 5 most semantically similar documents using the cosine distance operator <=>.

data.text: Choosing an Index and a Distance Operator

pgvector supports three distance operators: `<->` for L2, `<#>` for negative inner product, and `<=>` for cosine distance. The operator must match the index operator class, or the planner ignores the index. HNSW indexes give the best recall and query speed and support incremental inserts; IVFFlat builds faster and uses less memory but needs a representative sample of data before the index is built and must be re-created as the data grows.

data.title: An HNSW index and a nearest-neighbour query
data.content: `vector_cosine_ops` pairs with the `<=>` operator; ordering by distance and limiting to a few rows is what the index accelerates.

data.title: Interview angle: pgvector vs a dedicated vector database
data.text: pgvector keeps embeddings in the same database as the rest of your data, so you can filter by tenant, join to product rows, and get transactional consistency in one query. A dedicated vector store such as Pinecone or Milvus scales to billions of vectors and offers distributed search, but adds another system to operate and keep in sync. For most applications under a few million vectors, pgvector is the simpler and often faster-to-ship choice; the trade-off to name is recall tuning versus operational simplicity.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `pgvector` eliminates the need for separate standalone vector databases like Pinecone.
Use `HNSW` indexes for superior recall speed and accuracy.
The `<=>` operator computes cosine distance; `<->` computes Euclidean (L2) distance.
